I've read fm.md, agents.md, the handover, the linker (`tools/fmlink.py`), and a spread of nodes — the loop spec, the scope lattice, messaging, and the auto-update policy node. The audit runs clean. Here's my honest read, design-level.

## What I think is genuinely working

**The provenance discipline is the most novel thing here, more than the composition mechanics.** Every node cites the prompt that caused it, `audit_prompts.py` inverts that into a reverse index, and the audit currently shows zero orphans. Requirements traceability is usually enterprise theater that decays in weeks; here it holds because agents write everything and the transcript *is* the requirements document. The codebase is effectively a materialized conversation, and the tree is its table of contents. That's a real idea, and I don't think fm.md fully claims it yet — the doctrine sells user-controllable feature sets, but what you've actually built is closer to *provenance-modular* architecture, where the unit of code is the unit of conversational intent. The toggle test ("a feature that cannot be turned off is not a feature yet") is what makes it falsifiable rather than aspirational — most "modular" architectures never once test removal.

**The linker punches way above its 680 lines.** Two decisions carry it. First, offloading overload dispatch to rustc via generated traits (`fmlink.py:351`) — the linker does zero type inference and you still get real multiple dispatch with real type checking. Second, the per-line source map that rewrites rustc diagnostics back to `feature-file:line` (`report_diagnostics`), plus the `translate()` that rephrases trait-bound errors in fm terms. That's the moment fmlink stops being a concatenator and becomes an actual linker. And the same composition model — linearise, inject at extension points, provenance-comment — spans Rust chains, struct merge, and page fragments at slot markers. One mental model across three languages is the difference between an architecture and a pile of conventions.

**`auto.js` is a lovely worked example.** The typeof-guard idiom ("absence is the unticked state"), the wrap-the-parent's-function extension, the inherent reload-loop guard, and the spec's insistence that the on/off switch is inclusion itself rather than a config flag — policy-as-node is the doctrine actually cashing out.

## Where I see load-bearing tensions

**The regex parser vs. the `.lib.rs` escape hatch is a slow-motion fork.** No commas in parameter types means no generics in chain functions, so anything type-rich migrates to verbatim libraries where the composition machinery — chains, `existing`, toggling at function granularity — doesn't reach. `Var<T>` is already there. Each rung on the handover ladder (typed state, typed message routing) pushes more code toward the typed side. Worth watching the ratio of lib-lines to chain-lines over time: if it climbs steadily, the linker's parse layer needs to grow up (a real syn-based parse, or the v2 generation pass) before the interesting code has all escaped the model. The handover's "typed message routing via v2 linker generation" suggests you already feel this.

**Chain identity is positional, and nothing tools that.** What `existing` resolves to depends on linearisation order, which depends on tree shape plus order.md. agents.md warns that regrouping can reorder extension chains, but the protection is "relink and test." A `fmlink --chains` dump (chain key → ordered list of feature names) that you can diff before/after a reorganisation would be cheap insurance — especially since the 4–6 child cap *forces* regroups (shell is at the cap now), so reorganisation is a planned event, not an accident.

**fm.md and the implementation have quietly diverged on struct merge.** The doctrine describes namespaced fields (`colour.colour.r` / `colour.alpha.a`); `merge_structs` does a flat merge where a duplicate field name is a link error. Flat is honestly the better call at this scale — but it means two independent features can collide on a field name with no scoping to save them. Reporting per the errata rule, since fm.md is yours to edit. (Same category as the already-noted ordering-section/products divergence.)

**One-prompt-per-node has no depth control.** The 4–6 cap fights breadth, but refinements-become-subfeatures means bug fixes stack: a fix to a fix lands three deep, and in a year some chains will be a base plus five sedimentary layers, each individually toggleable but not meaningfully so — nobody will ever untick "the fix from August." Breadth has a sanctioned repair (the regroup); depth may eventually want its analog — a sanctioned *absorb*, where a stack of refinements collapses into its parent, with the provenance trail surviving in the transcript citations rather than the tree shape. Not urgent at 56 nodes; worth having a doctrine answer before it's urgent.

**Small code notes**, none alarming at current scale: the broadcast slot is a single `/tmp` JSON file with a 50-entry ring and a 200ms poll loop per waiting thread — right-sized for a three-device fleet, and the server-side audience filter in `wait_filter` is the correct place for that check. The `_send` queue smuggled through the state JSON is pragmatic, but it's an untyped protocol hiding inside an opaque string — exactly the thing "typed state" (rung 4) should formalize.

## Overall

Two days in, this is a coherent system with an unusually honest discipline around it — agents.md reads like it was written by someone who watched the failure mode happen, which per its own footnote it was. The thing I'd most want to protect as it grows is the property that made the three-way tap demo satisfying: that every behaviour on screen can be walked back to a sentence someone typed. The threats to that property aren't in the tree rules — they're in the escape hatches (`.lib.rs`, tools/, the explorer-template debt the audit already flags). The debt is known and listed, which is itself a good sign.

Happy to dig into any of these — the chain-dump tool and the depth question are the two I'd argue are worth a conversation before the next growth spurt.

### p8
*2026-08-14 12:20*

> explain the chain dump concisely please?

When several features redefine the same function, they form a chain — and which `existing` calls which is determined purely by linearisation order, which is determined by tree shape plus order.md. That wiring is currently invisible: it exists only inside the linker while it runs.

The chain dump is a flag (`fmlink.py muon --chains`) that prints that wiring and stops:

```
route(request) -> response:
  serve → users/gate → comms/messaging → diag
render():
  shell → shell/logo
update(String, String) -> String:
  loop → loop/tap
```

Each line is one chain key (name + parameter types) followed by the features that extend it, in order — innermost first, outermost last.

The point is diffability. When you regroup a subtree (as the shell cap will soon force), the linearisation can change, which can silently rewire who wraps whom. Dump before, dump after, diff: an unchanged diff proves the regroup was purely organisational; a changed diff shows exactly which chains rewired, before anything ships. It turns "relink and test" into evidence.

Cost: the linker already builds this structure in `compose_features` — it's ~15 lines of printing.

### p9
*2026-08-14 12:22*

> Hm, that's an interesting oversight on my part. It means regrouping features will change their ordering, which will obviously change behaviour (unless there's a lot of parallelism). I wonder if there's a way we can stabilise ordering even in the face of regrouping?

This touches something already latent in the design. The original decision (notes.md, 2026-08-13) was "ordering = creation time" — order.md just materialises chronology by appending on creation. The known consequence noted back then was exactly this: DFS traversal breaks *global* chronology across subtrees (with A → [B, C], B → [D]: linearisation is A, B, D, C — so C wraps D even though D is newer). Regrouping is just the acute version of that ambient problem.

I see three candidate stabilisations, in ascending order of ambition:

**1. Discipline + evidence (the current plan).** Keep DFS ordering; require regroups to preserve linearisation, verified by an empty chain-dump diff. Cheap, but it stabilises by vigilance, not by construction — and it forbids regroups that *should* move things.

**2. A chain lockfile.** Separate ordering from grouping explicitly: the linker maintains a checked-in manifest of each chain's member order (essentially the chain dump promoted from diagnostic to source of truth). The tree then controls only inclusion; regrouping can't touch behaviour by construction. Works, but it's a second ordering artifact to maintain alongside order.md.

**3. Linearise by provenance timestamp, not tree position.** Every node already carries the timestamp of the prompt that caused it. Make *that* the linearisation order: the transcript is the true program order, and the tree becomes a pure grouping/selection view with no behavioural weight at all. Regrouping then cannot change behaviour, by construction, with no new artifact — the ordering data already exists in every node.

Option 3 is the one I find striking, because of what falls out:

- **"Newest is outermost" becomes globally true**, restoring the original intent that DFS quietly broke. Later refinements wrap earlier behaviour, always.
- **The #p91 constraint dissolves.** "An extension must linearise after its base — tree position bounds what a node can own" becomes "you can extend anything that existed when you were written." That's causality, not tree-shape accident — and it un-blocks the case you hit where `serve/features` couldn't extend gate's chains because of DFS position. Cross-cutting features get dramatically easier.
- It's the provenance-modularity thesis made mechanical: composition order = order of intent.

Costs to be honest about: chronology is occasionally the *wrong* order (you'd want a rare, explicit per-node override — "linearise before X" — rather than today's implicit edit-order.md); order.md's role shrinks to catalog + selection (which #p132a was already pushing it toward); and the linker needs to read timestamps from provenance anchors, which is real but small work since transcripts record them under every `#pN`.

Notably, the chain dump is step zero for all three options — even under provenance ordering you want to see the chains, and migrating to option 3 needs a before/after diff of exactly that kind.

This is a doctrine-level change, so it's yours to call. Want me to write the three options up as a proposal in notes.md while it's fresh?

### p13
*2026-08-14 12:44*

> describe the shell regroup?

Shell is at the 6-child cap — `order.md` reads: logo, update, icon, install, pinned, panel. The rule says the *next* child forces a reorganisation, so the regroup is about doing it deliberately now, with evidence, rather than mid-feature later.

**What the six children are:** logo (the ᕦ(ツ)ᕤ mark + raise), update (the whole build-awareness stack: buildnum, fresh, honest, watch, auto), icon (PWA icons + everypage head links), install (the install wall + steps), pinned (standalone-app chrome CSS), panel (the corner system UI: button, lozenge, corner, source).

**The natural grouping:** icon, install, and pinned are all one concept — *being an installed PWA*: the manifest/icon identity, the add-to-home-screen wall, the standalone chrome. Group them as `shell/pwa` (or `installed`):

```
shell → logo, update, pwa{icon, install, pinned}, panel
```

That takes shell from 6 children to 4, with room to grow, and the grouping node is legal by the rules: grouping nodes may be code-free, and fm.md explicitly allows a regroup node to skip the provenance prompt (it cites the 4–6 rule instead). The alternatives I considered are weaker: `brand{logo, icon}` splits icon from install, which are more related to each other than to logo; and `sysui{panel, update}` couples two things that interact but aren't one concept.

**Why this particular grouping is safe:** icon, install, pinned are *contiguous* in order.md (positions 3–5), and wrapping a contiguous run in a group node while keeping internal order preserves DFS linearisation exactly — so by construction, no chain rewires. The `--chains` diff before/after should be empty, and that's the verification step.

**One gap the regroup exposes:** `--chains` covers Rust chains only, but these three nodes are mostly *fragments* (CSS/JS injected at page slots), and fragments also compose in linearisation order — CSS cascade order is behaviour too. So before doing the regroup, I'd extend the dump to also print fragment order per page/slot. Small addition, same shape as the chain print, and it makes the "empty diff" claim honest for the fragment-heavy shell subtree.

**Mechanics:** create `features/muon/shell/pwa/` with a short grouping spec, `git mv` the three folders in, give pwa an order.md (icon, install, pinned), shrink shell's order.md to four lines. The muon product needs nothing — it symlinks `features/muon` wholesale. Then dump-diff, relink, run the toggle test on one moved node, deploy.

If proposal 9 lands first, the safety argument becomes moot — chronology makes any regroup order-neutral. But the fragment-dump gap is worth closing either way, since fragments will need a chronology story too.

Want me to do it — fragment dump first, then the regroup?

### p16
*2026-08-14 12:55*

> One way to get around the depth issue is to have a "two-phase" approach to features. When we first create a feature, we'll expect a bunch of churn, and nobody else is using the feature, so it's safe to make big changes to it. This is a strong resolution — it reframes the depth problem as a lifecycle question. Let me capture it with a proper anchor first.

Recorded in notes.md and committed (`b9c48b5`) — hygiene item 7 resolved in principle, which clears the whole board: five done, one pinned, none open.

I think this is the right resolution, and the reason is worth stating: it exposes that subfeature-per-refinement was always a *compatibility* mechanism masquerading as a history mechanism. History is already covered twice over — transcripts and git. The only thing a refinement subtree buys is that someone else can decline the change by toggling it — and while a feature has no other consumers, that machinery serves no one. Your instinct that the depth pressure felt artificial was accurate: with one user, everything in the tree is effectively still draft.

A few consequences I recorded:

- **"Immutable except refactoring" resolves cleanly as: the spec freezes, the code doesn't quite.** Published means the spec is the contract; the implementation may still move *toward* it (bug fixes) or preserve behaviour under it (the existing refactoring rule, backed by tests). ### p19
*2026-08-14 13:14*

> so I noticed with the tap thing; say I have two instances running, and they both have 0 taps. if I tap either of them, the tap counts sync between instances. If however I restart one of the instances, its tap count goes to zero, so we're now out of sync.

That's handover rung 1 showing itself — "vars converge on writes only; a relaunching device forgets" — and it's a good concrete entry into the distribution conversation, because the bug is really a missing quarter of the authority model.

**Why it happens:** state lives in the page and round-trips through the wasm loop; `boot()` builds it from `init()`, which yields `{}`, so `Var::get` returns `Default` — zero taps. The server still holds the authoritative total (the file-backed store), but nothing *pulls* it at boot: convergence only travels on writes. When anyone taps, the server publishes the new total and every long-polling instance — including the restarted one — snaps back to truth. So the system self-heals on the next write anywhere, but until then the restarted instance sits at zero, lying.

Put in the terms of your day-one placement doctrine: a freshly booted instance is just *a replica that is maximally behind*. The doctrine says functions always work against a local replica and reconciliation always exists — but the reconciliation path currently only covers the steady state (broadcast deltas), not the join. Hydration is the missing catch-up half, and it's worth designing as such, because the *same* mechanism is what an offline device needs on reconnect. Boot-after-restart and reconnect-after-tunnel-outage are one problem: "my replica is stale by an unknown amount."

The design I'd argue for:

1. **Hydration arrives as events through the normal loop, not as a state overwrite.** After boot, the client sends `{type:"Hydrate"}` up the existing message pipe; the server replies with the current values of every var in the scopes that client can hear (global + `user:me` — the same audience filter `wait_filter` already enforces, so nothing leaks). The values come back as the same `VarSync`-shaped events the broadcast path already delivers, injected through `on_event`. That keeps two properties intact: features handle their own keys with code they already have, and the blackbox records hydration like any other input — so replay of a restarted instance stays deterministic.

2. **Snapshot semantics, not ring catch-up.** The broadcast ring holds 50 entries and truncates, so "replay everything since v=0" can't be the join mechanism. The server's var store *is* the snapshot; hydrate reads it directly. (The ring stays what it is: live-delta transport.)

3. **Later, local-first polish:** persist last-known-good state in the page (localStorage) so a restarted instance shows its previous count *immediately* and then converges when hydration lands — rather than flashing zero. That's the "cache serves while the network catches up" principle you already established at the HTTP layer, applied to state.

Steps 1+2 are a small amount of work — a `Hydrate` handler on the server's `handle_msg` chain next to the existing var machinery, and a client-side send after boot — and they unblock the runtime per-user policy toggles that auto-update's spec is waiting on. As a node it's presumably `loop/scope/hydrate` (a refinement of scope).

### p20
*2026-08-14 13:16*

> explain the term "hydrate"?

It's a borrowed term from web development, and the metaphor is "adding water back to something dried out."

The original use: server-side rendering sends a browser static HTML — the *dehydrated* form of an app: correct shape, no life. The framework then attaches event handlers and live state to that markup so it becomes interactive. That attach step got called **hydration** — reconstituting a living thing from its dried form, like instant coffee or a freeze-dried meal.

By extension it now means, generally: **filling an empty or skeletal structure with its real values from the authoritative source**. An ORM "hydrates" an object from database rows; a cache "hydrates" from the backing store.

In our case: a restarted muon instance has the dried form — the code, the state shape, `Var` declarations that all read as `Default` — and hydration is the boot-time step where the server's authoritative values get poured back in, so the replica is live and current rather than structurally correct but empty.

If the metaphor doesn't sit right for fm's vocabulary, the plainer name for what I proposed is a **catch-up** or **sync-on-join** — which arguably describes the mechanism better, since the same act serves both boot and reconnect. Glossary choice is yours; the concept is just "new replica asks the authority for current truth before trusting its defaults."

### p21
*2026-08-14 13:17*

> let's call it "join" - we're "joining a session". Which raises the question: should we have some kind of a session object?

"Join" is better — I'll use that. And the session-object question is exactly where your day-one notes left a tension worth confronting, because you've already taken a position once: the SCOPE discussion (#p129) concluded *"sessions/rooms fall out of scoping rather than existing separately"* — sessions as emergent, not objects. The join protocol tests whether that position survives contact.

Here's how I'd split it. "Session" is overloading two different things:

**The durable axis — who *may* hear.** That's the scope lattice, and it's already answered: a session in the "room" sense is just a Group scope key. Membership, invitation, leaving — that's the group membership model (handover rung 2), and it's data, not a new primitive.

**The ephemeral axis — who *is here now*.** This is presence: which replicas are currently live, current, and listening. Scoping genuinely does *not* give you this, and it's the part join creates. But before reaching for an object, notice what presence actually is: **server-derived state**. An instance cannot truthfully maintain its own presence — a crashed replica can't write its departure. The server already *has* the truth (it holds the long-polls); presence is a read-out of connection state, not a thing instances write.

So my answer to "should we have a session object?": **not as a new primitive — but yes as a first-class *view* built from three parts you mostly already have:**

1. **Instance identity.** This is the real missing noun. Today identity stops at the user; your phone and your browser tab are indistinguishable replicas. Join is the natural moment to mint a durable per-instance id (persisted locally, presented on every join). Note this also completes the scope lattice's bottom rung — `Local` scope is really *per-instance* scope, and now it has a key.
2. **The join act**: instance presents (user cookie, instance id, scope subscriptions) → server registers it live and returns the snapshot of hearable vars — the catch-up we discussed, plus an implicit "you are now present."
3. **Presence as server-published state**: the server maintains the live-instance table from joins and long-poll lapses, and publishes it *as an ordinary scoped var* (e.g. a user-scoped or group-scoped map of instance → last-seen). Features that want "who's here" just read a var like any other — no new machinery on the consuming side, blackbox-recordable like everything else.

The session "object", then, is the pair (scope key, presence var) — a thing you can talk about and render, built entirely from existing primitives plus the one genuinely new noun, the instance id. That keeps the #p129 insight intact while giving join something concrete to join.

The pleasing consequence: single-user multi-device (your three-screen tap demo) and multi-user collaboration become literally the same mechanism at different scope levels — user-scope presence vs group-scope presence. And your multi-device "one surface" use case from #p35 gets its foundation — the colour-picker-on-phone scenario needs exactly instance identity + presence to say "render the picker on *that* replica."

### p30
*2026-08-14 17:37*

> back from my nap, refreshed :-) OK so. Question: is it possible for us to push state silently to a muon instance that's not in the foreground?

Welcome back :-) Let me ground the answer in what the push machinery actually does today:

Short answer: **truly silent, no — but usefully close, yes.** The constraint is Apple's, not ours. Breakdown by instance situation:

**Backgrounded iOS PWA**: its JavaScript is frozen — the long-poll is dead, timers dead, nothing executes. The *only* thing that can wake any of your code is a Web Push, and iOS's rule is hard: every push must produce a user-visible notification. There's no `silent: true` for web push; Safari tracks pushes that don't show a notification and revokes the subscription after a few violations. Android/Chrome nominally has the same `userVisibleOnly` requirement, just enforced more leniently. So "push state without the user noticing" is exactly the thing the platform forbids — by design, since silent wake = covert background execution.

**But here's the useful loophole**: the push *does* wake the service worker with up to ~4KB of (already-encrypted — your RFC 8291 pipeline) payload, and the SW may do work in `waitUntil` *before* showing the notification — including writing to Cache Storage or IndexedDB. So you **can** push state to the *device* silently; you just can't push it to the device *invisibly*. The pattern: piggyback state on notifications you were sending anyway. The deploy announcement could carry the current var snapshot; the SW stashes it; the app's next launch joins *from local storage instantly*, then confirms with the server. Combined with your nap-time request — join gating first paint — that's an app that opens already-current with zero flash and zero wait, even after days closed.

**Backgrounded desktop tab**: different story — long-polls survive backgrounding (timers get throttled, but an in-flight fetch keeps waiting), so those instances stay warm already.

**Closed instance**: nothing runs, nothing can run; the stashed-payload trick above is the whole story.

One genuine gap this question surfaced, worth its own note: **resume is a stale moment we don't join on.** When an iOS PWA comes back to foreground after a long suspension, the long-poll resumes with `since = lastV` — but the broadcast ring only holds 50 entries, so a long-enough absence has a hole in it, and unlike boot, resume never sends a Join. The fix is one line of concept: *foregrounding after suspension is a join moment too* — visibilitychange → queue a Join. Cheap, honest, and it makes "join = catch-up whenever you might be stale" fully general (boot, reconnect, resume).

So the menu, cheapest first: (a) **resume-join** — closes a real correctness hole today; (b) **snapshot-on-notification** — state piggybacked on pushes you already send, stashed by the SW; (c) accept that "silent + backgrounded + iOS" is a platform wall nobody gets through, PWA or native (even native apps get only ~summary background pushes with system-throttled delivery).

What's driving the question — instant-open freshness, or something for located posts?

> should we institute a convention that feature names (i.e. the file + title names) have to be unique across the tree and summarise what they do, rather than depending on their parent feature names?

Yes — and I'd argue proposal 9 already made the decision quietly. Here's the reasoning:

**The namespace is already flat where it matters.** Struct names are tree-global (`feature_Gate` collided across unrelated subtrees today), and JS is worse: two page fragments declaring `const feature_Gate` is a `SyntaxError` that kills *every* script on the page — and the linker doesn't catch it, only rustc caught the Rust half. The implementation layer has always been a flat namespace; path-scoped node names were writing checks the composition layer can't cash.

**Provenance ordering finished the job.** Since the tree carries grouping and selection only, a node's real identity is its name + its timestamp; the path is presentation. Names that only make sense in path context ("gate", "pwa", "auto") are anchored to something the architecture now says is freely rearrangeable. A name should survive its node being regrouped — which means it must stand alone.

**And sharing will demand it.** The two-phase lifecycle points at features moving between users. "gate" travels badly; "join-gate" is self-carrying. Same for glossary `/term` links and plain conversation — `/gate` is ambiguous in your own tree today.

Current collisions and near-collisions, for concreteness: **`pwa`** twice (`shell/pwa` the installed-app group, `diag/pwa` the standalone-mode detector) and **`gate`** twice (`users/gate` auth, `join/gate` the paint veil). Sensible renames keep the older/primary holder and rename the junior: `diag/pwa` → `standalone`, `join/gate` → `veil` (which is honestly a better name anyway — descriptive without the parent's help). Notably, **renames are now behaviour-free**: chains key on struct names and timestamps, provenance is citations, so renaming a folder can't rewire anything — this is the cheapest moment there will ever be to adopt the rule.

The convention I'd propose, if you bless it:

1. **A node's name is globally unique across the tree** and describes its capability without needing the path (path adds organisation, never meaning).
2. **One name, three forms**: folder/file `join-gate`-style, spec title matching, struct `feature_JoinGate` derived mechanically. (Bikeshed: whether folders use `joingate`, `join-gate`, or `veil`-style fresh words — I lean toward fresh, evocative single words where they exist, compound only when needed.)
3. **The linker enforces it** — duplicate node names anywhere in an included tree = link error, code-free nodes included. That's the part that catches the silent JS death.

This is a tree rule, so it's fm.md territory — yours to write; I'd record the decision in notes.md meanwhile. Want me to go ahead with the enforcement check and the two renames?

### p34
*2026-08-14 18:04*

> ok, so shall we talk about data places a bit?

Yes — let's. I'll lay out where I think the ground is, and the three tensions I'd want your instincts on. The standing doctrine (from day one, #p34/#p37) is: *code is placeless, data has places; features declare needs and constraints, products declare topology; semantics are pinned at the distributed end so colocation is only an optimisation.* That's held up well. But building join/veil/resume against it today exposed some structure underneath it that the doctrine hasn't named yet.

**1. "Place" is currently two different things.** places.md declares `server` and `client` — but those are *place-kinds* (build targets). At runtime, one kind multiplies: there are three running instances of `client` in your tap demo, and they are *distinct places* — each has its own replica, its own staleness, its own Local scope. The instance-identity noun we deferred from the join discussion is actually the runtime half of the places vocabulary: **place-kind** (declared, in places.md, what the linker builds) vs **place** (a running instance with an identity, an inventory, and a connection state). The vocabulary needs both, and today only the first exists.

**2. Var<T> quietly conflates three axes that places must split.** When you write `Var::global("tap_count")`, one word is deciding three separate questions:

- **Scope** — *who may see it* (the audience/access axis: Local/User/Group/Global). This is settled and good.
- **Authority** — *which place holds the truth*. Today: always the server, for everything. Invisible because there's only one candidate.
- **Replication** — *which places hold copies, and how eagerly*. Today: every hearing client, eagerly, via broadcast+join.

These coincide for a tap counter. They *don't* coincide for the data your real app wants. Which brings me to —

**3. The walk documenter is the forcing case, and it breaks the current defaults beautifully.** Trace its data journey: 360° stills are born on the phone — gigabytes, **User-scoped but device-authoritative** (the server doesn't have them and can't; the phone owns the truth for hours, possibly offline the whole walk). Then authority *migrates*: upload moves truth to the server. Then a **compute place** appears — splat/mesh building wants a big machine; that's a place-kind that exists to run one expensive function near the data, something places.md has no word for. Then the finished model is Group- or Global-scoped, server-authoritative, **lazily replicated** — nobody eagerly pushes a 200MB splat to every phone; viewers fetch on demand, maybe thumbnails eagerly. Every axis that Var collapses, this app needs pulled apart. And none of it is exotic — it's just "posts with media."

So the shape I'd propose for the vocabulary — as a discussion seed, not a conclusion: a **store** is a named, typed collection carrying four independent declarations: *scope* (who may hear — exists today), *authority* (which place-kind holds truth — new, currently hardwired "server"), *replication policy* (eager / lazy / on-demand / never — new, currently hardwired "eager to all hearers"), and *representation* (the typed-state rung). `Var<T>` becomes the degenerate store: single value, server-authoritative, eager. The next store type the app needs is a **blob store** (content-addressed, lazy). Features declare which stores they need and the constraints ("never leaves the device", "must live somewhere trusted"); the product's places.md grows a data section binding stores to homes; the linker validates constraints against topology, as #p37 always promised. And join/veil/resume generalize per-store: what we built today is the catch-up protocol *for the Var store*; each store type owns its own staleness answer.

The three questions I'd most like your read on:

1. Does **authority migration** (phone-truth → server-truth at upload) deserve to be a first-class act in the vocabulary, or is it just "two stores and a copy"?
2. Is a **compute place** a real place-kind (an inventory that includes "lots of cores/GPU" as a resource), or is that overreach — just a server function?
3. **Scope and place are near-duplicates in the small** (Local scope ≈ "this place only") — do we unify them (placement as the bottom of the scope lattice) or keep access and locality as strictly separate axes?

Where do you want to dig?

**The canvassing scenario, traced:** you're on a lane with no signal. You need to (a) *add* — "resident at #14 fed up with potholes" — and (b) *match* — "is there already anything about potholes near here?" Both must work offline, which dictates the whole data design:

**Posts want to be immutable, append-only facts.** A post is `{author, time, location, kind, content}` — and once made, it never changes. This one commitment dissolves most of the distribution problem: **append-only data has no write conflicts.** Two canvassers reporting the same pothole isn't a conflict to reconcile — it's two true facts that a later *match link* ("these describe the same pothole") connects, and links are additive, so they're conflict-free too. Your question 1 answer falls out: **authority migration mostly dissolves here.** A post is born authoritative on the phone and stays true forever; the server isn't the owner of truth, it's the *exchange* — copies propagate, nothing migrates. Authority only matters for the mutable minority: aggregates ("100 fixed this month"), moderation, edits-as-retractions. Compare the walk documenter, where a mutable 200MB artifact genuinely needs an authoritative home — the two apps stress opposite ends, which is exactly what a vocabulary wants from its test cases.

**Matching offline forces the interesting axis: replication by interest.** You can't hold the whole spatial database on a phone; you must hold *your patch*. So the store needs a spatial key (tiles/geohash), and replication policy becomes: **eager within my subscribed tiles, on-demand elsewhere.** And here's the resolution to my question 3, concretely: what reaches your device is the intersection of two key-set subscriptions — **scope** (what you *may* hear: canvassing data is sensitive, so team-scoped, not public) and **interest** (what you *care* about: tiles around your patch). Access and locality stay separate axes, but they're the *same mechanism* — the broadcast audience filter you already have, generalised from `{global, user.me}` to a subscription set `{team.X, tile.A..F}`. Notice tiles behave exactly like ad-hoc groups — which means the group-membership rung and spatial subscription are plausibly **one design**, and this app finally makes rung 2 urgent for real.

**Question 2 also simplifies: no compute place needed.** Matching v0 is distance + keywords over the local patch replica, on-device. Aggregates are cheap server jobs. Defer.

**And the infrastructure you already have maps on almost embarrassingly well.** Offline add = the persistent outbox (built, day 2). Sync-on-signal = resume/online join (built, today). Never-lie-about-staleness = veil + the honesty banner — which for this app should grow one word: "showing your patch, last synced 2h ago." Patchy-network canvassing is the environment muon's whole client stack has been unknowingly built for.

So the muon-level shape this asks for — the first real store beyond `Var<T>`: an **append-only, spatially-keyed, scope-audienced item log with interest-based replication**. And a probe ladder where each rung is small: (1) immutable located posts through the existing outbox, server as exchange, naive full replication — the three-device demo becomes "post a pothole on the phone, see it on the laptop"; (2) tile keys + interest subscription — replication becomes partial; (3) offline round-trip proven in airplane mode; (4) a map/list explorer; (5) matching v0 = "nearby similar posts" at capture time. Group scope slots in when the team stops being "just you."

The two design commitments I'd want you to actually bless before we build, since everything downstream leans on them: **posts are immutable (edits are new posts / retractions are links)**, and **replication = scope ∩ interest as key-set subscription**. Do both sit right? And does the aggregate kind ("100 fixed this month") need to be first-class from the start, or is it a later derived-view story?

> the other part I didn't mention is that we want to perform agentic interrogation of the dataset. in other words, when we're in a voter conversation about potholes, we want to be - in the background - using an agent to surface relevant points that we can use in our conversation. And again, that has to work offline if there's no network.

Noted in ideas.md. And here's the thing — this requirement is the places doctrine's finest hour, because #p34 already contains the sentence that handles it: *"offline shrinks reachable places, but functions with local data keep running."* The agent is just a function with data needs. Let me decompose it honestly, because "agent, offline, on a phone, in a PWA" hides three very different sub-problems:

**Decomposed, "surface relevant points" is a pipeline:** *query formation* (what is this conversation about? — v0: the canvasser taps a topic chip or types two words; ambient speech-to-text is heavy and can come later) → *retrieval* (find relevant posts in the patch — this is where most of the value lives) → *synthesis* (turn them into talking points — the "agentic" garnish).

**The key move: enrich at the exchange, consume at the edge.** Embedding the *corpus* is the heavy compute, but it doesn't need to happen on the phone or at use time — the server embeds each post *once, at sync time*, and the embedding replicates **with** the post as part of the patch. Offline, the device only embeds the *query* (a small embedding model runs fine in wasm/WebGPU — hundreds of MB, not GB) and does a nearest-neighbour search over its patch replica — thousands of vectors, milliseconds. Same pattern one level up: the server's agent can precompute **tile digests** at sync time — "talking points for this area" — which replicate with the patch and give you real agentic value offline with *zero* on-device inference, honestly stamped "as of last sync, 2h ago". In places vocabulary: these are **derived stores** (posts → embeddings → digests), computed where compute is cheap, replicated by the same interest set as their source.

**Synthesis gets a degradation ladder, not a requirement.** Online: the full server-side agent, live. Offline on a capable device: a small local model (real but marginal in a PWA today — WebGPU inference works in Safari 26 and a ~1B quantized model is feasible, but Safari's per-tab memory ceiling makes 3B-class models dicey, and battery matters when you're canvassing all day). Offline floor, always available: **retrieval + digests, no synthesis** — show the five most relevant posts and the area digest. I'd argue the floor is 80% of the field value: a canvasser mid-conversation wants *"3 pothole reports on this road, council fixed 100 last month, resident at #9 raised the same thing"* — that's retrieval, not generation. The ladder is the freshness doctrine applied to intelligence: degrade visibly, never fail silently, never lie about what you're working from.

**What this adds to the places vocabulary** — two things, both already latent in the doctrine: (1) **derived stores** with a compute-place annotation — "computed at X from Y, replicated like Y"; (2) **place capabilities as dispatchable resources** — a place's inventory includes "has model M" / "has GPU", and the synthesis function has variants keyed by resource type, exactly the mechanism #p35 proposed for `render(s: touch_surface)` vs `render(s: main_surface)`. The ladder isn't an if-else in app code; it's multiple dispatch over what the current place can satisfy. The doctrine predicted its own use case.

One PWA-honesty flag for the record: the retrieval floor and digests are comfortably within PWA reach; the *local-LLM* rung is the one place where "muon is a PWA" may eventually chafe against "canvass all day on a phone," and if it does, that's a product-topology decision (a native-wrapped place-kind) — not an architecture change, which is rather the point of the doctrine.

Design-wise I think the picture is now coherent enough to write down: the post store (immutable, tiled, scope∩interest replication), derived stores, the enrichment-at-exchange pattern, and the synthesis ladder. Shall I record it in notes.md as the places-conversation outcome so far — and do the two commitments from before (immutable posts, subscription-based replication) plus these get your blessing as the working design?

> let's slow down a bit. I'm having a conversation with a voter (holding the phone up dictaphone-style so they know I'm note-taking) - the audio is recording, and there's transcription/dictation running in parallel. If we're connected to the server with sufficient bandwidth, we can stream the audio up to the server, which returns the transcription. If we're not connected (or connection is too slow) we have to perform the transciption on the device, and then *later* upload for a higher-quality transcription. That's the thing I'd like to be able to express concisely, because it's the pattern for lots of things that need to happen.

Good — this is the right thing to slow down on, because what you've described is one pattern wearing many faces, and it deserves a name and a one-line expression. Let me try to say it back precisely:

**The audio is the fact; the transcript is a derivation.** The recording is captured locally, immutable, born on the device — that part is settled vocabulary. The transcript is *derived* data with more than one way to derive it: a **ranked set of implementations** — call them rungs — each with declared needs:

```
derive transcript from audio:
    transcribe(a: Audio, m: server_model) -> Text    // best; needs the exchange, within budget
    transcribe(a: Audio, m: device_model) -> Text    // floor; needs nothing
```

And then the whole behaviour you described is one standing rule:

> **Run the best rung whose needs are reachable *now*; stamp the result with the rung that made it; when a better rung comes into reach, re-run and upgrade the value in place.**

Walk your scenario through it: connected with bandwidth → the top rung's needs are satisfied, audio streams up, server text streams back. Lane with no signal → the reachable set shrinks (the #p34 sentence again), the floor rung runs, you get device-quality text stamped *provisional*. Signal returns → the audio replicates to the exchange (ordinary interest-based replication of the immutable fact — "upload" isn't special), the server re-derives, and the better transcript flows back down as an ordinary value-update through the loop; the note upgrades itself in front of you. Nothing in that last act is new machinery — it's the derived-store rule doing its job: *derived data re-computes at the best place that can, and replicates like its source*.

Three parts of this are genuinely new vocabulary; everything else exists:

1. **Ranked rungs.** The mechanism is multiple dispatch over resource types — which fm already has, signature-keyed — plus an ordering. The ranking *is* the declaration.
2. **Reachability with a budget.** "Connected" isn't boolean — your own freshness-deadline principle, generalised from HTTP caching to places: *a place is reachable for a purpose if it can serve it within that purpose's deadline*. Live dictation has a per-chunk budget; a slow link fails the budget and the floor rung takes over mid-conversation — and can switch back, per chunk, as the link breathes.
3. **Provisionality as honest metadata.** Every derived value carries its rung. The UI can render draft-ness (dimmed text, a small mark) and the upgrade moment; the honesty doctrine extends from "never lie about freshness" to **"never lie about quality."**

And you're right that it's the pattern for lots of things — it's the same shape as the synthesis ladder from the agent discussion (cloud agent / local model / retrieval floor), same as embedding (device embeds query cheaply now; exchange embeds corpus richly at sync), same as the future splat pipeline (phone preview mesh now, big-machine splat later), even the same as the veil (local state now, joined state moments later — join is just this pattern applied to *state* rather than compute). One rule, declared per derivation, enforced by the runtime.

Name candidates for the doctrine: I'd call the whole thing a **graded derivation** ("derive at the best reachable rung; provisional results upgrade"), with **rung** for each implementation and **budget** for the reachability test. If the name and shape sit right, I'll record it in notes.md as the central finding of the places conversation — it's compact enough to be the thing places.md's data section is eventually built around.
